lesson_title: Two Piles, One Answer: Resultants by the Component Method
hook_text: Walk 60 metres east, 80 metres north. You walked 140 metres — but you are only 100 metres from home. That gap is the whole topic.
clip_script: Walk 60 metres east, then 80 metres north. Your feet did 140 metres. But a bird flying straight from your gate to you flies only 100. That straight flight is the RESULTANT — the one trip that does the job of all the others. Now the hard part, and it is not hard. Someone drags a suitcase with the handle tilted up. That pull is doing two jobs at once: pulling forward AND lifting. So sort it, like a shopkeeper sorting mixed change into piles. One pile forward, one pile up. A 250 newton pull tilted 30 degrees gives 216,5 newtons forward and 125 newtons up. Do that to every force. Then add the sideways pile — remembering west is minus. Add the upward pile — remembering south is minus. Now you have two arrows at right angles, and that is the bird-flight problem again. Square them, add, square root: 235,7 newtons. Divide up by sideways, hit inverse tangent: 65 comma 8 degrees. Split, add, rebuild. Three moves. And never, ever hand in the number without the direction.
visual_style: A township street grid seen from above, a walking route lighting up in two straight legs with the diagonal snapping into place; then a tilted suitcase handle splitting into two glowing arrows; finally four messy arrows collapsing into two, then one.
mood: Brisk and reassuring — an intimidating topic quietly turning into bookkeeping.
pacing: Fast opening reveal, slow steady beat on the sorting, punchy three-word finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn any four forces into one clean answer.
